hints: Look at what atom or group replaces Br in reactions 1 and 3, and what small molecule is lost in reaction 2, to decide between substitution and elimination.
Remember that the solvent for NaOH or KOH controls the pathway, aqueous favours substitution to an alcohol while alcoholic favours elimination to an alkene.
Think about how carbon chain length changes, reaction 3 adds one carbon as $\text{CN}$, while reaction 4 keeps the same chain but converts $\text{CN}$ to $\text{COOH}$.
For nitrile hydrolysis in reaction 4, recall that dilute aqueous acid with heat converts $\text{RCN}$ to $\text{RCOOH}$.
For reactions 5 and 6, track oxidation level: $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{OH}$ to aldehyde to carboxylic acid, and recall the oxidising agent for primary alcohols.
Remember the key difference in conditions to stop at the aldehyde in reaction 5 versus going fully to the acid in reaction 6.
walkthrough:
Sort substitution versus elimination for the halogenoalkane**
Picture $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{Br}$. In reaction 1, $\text{Br}$ is swapped for $\text{OH}$ to give $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{OH}$. That is direct swapping, so think substitution. In reaction 2, $\text{HBr}$ is lost to form $\text{C=C}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. That is loss of a small molecule, so think elimination.

Use the solvent to choose the NaOH conditions**
This is the classic pair students mix up. Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, heated, acts as a nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$ and gives substitution. Ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$, heated, acts as a base and gives elimination. So reaction 1 needs aqueous, reaction 2 needs ethanolic.

Extend the chain with cyanide then hydrolyse**
In reaction 3, $\text{Br}$ is replaced by $\text{CN}$ to give $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. That is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^-$ from $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ in ethanol. In reaction 4 the nitrile becomes $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{COOH}$. Hydrolysis of $\text{RCN}$ needs dilute aqueous acid, such as dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, with heat.

Control the oxidation of the primary alcohol**
Reaction 5 is $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHO}$. That is partial oxidation to an aldehyde. You need acidified dichromate, $\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$, and you must distil off the aldehyde as soon as it forms so it cannot oxidise further. Reaction 6 is aldehyde to $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{COOH}$. That is further oxidation, so use acidified dichromate with reflux, or a mild oxidant like Tollens or Fehlings.

Final answer: Reaction 1: aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$ (or water, heat); substitution (hydrolysis).
Reaction 2: ethanolic / alcoholic $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$, heat; elimination.
Reaction 3: $\text{KCN}$ / $\text{NaCN}$ in ethanol / alcohol, heat; substitution.
Reaction 4: dilute aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$, heat; hydrolysis (substitution).
Reaction 5: acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ / $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ with distillation; oxidation (elimination).
Reaction 6: acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ (with reflux) OR Tollens / Fehlings / Benedicts; oxidation.

hints: Start from the nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$, identify where its lone pair attacks and why the carbon in $\text{C-Br}$ is electron deficient.
Recall what happens to the $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair when Br leaves, and how to show dipoles and charges on the transition.
walkthrough:
Show the nucleophile attacking**
Think of $\text{OH}^-$ with its full negative charge and lone pairs on oxygen. The carbon attached to Br is $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ because Br pulls electrons away. Draw a curly arrow starting at a lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ and pointing to that $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. This forms the new $\text{C-O}$ bond in one step, which is the heart of $\text{S}_\text{N}2$.

Show the leaving group leaving**
Now look at the $\text{C-Br}$ bond. Mark it $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to show polarity. As the $\text{O-C}$ bond forms, the $\text{C-Br}$ pair must go to Br. Draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br, giving $\text{Br}^-$. Both arrows happen together, no carbocation is formed.

Final answer: Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}$ of $\text{OH}^-$ to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C-Br}$.
$\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown with curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to give $\text{Br}^-$.

hints: Recall what stays the same in any type of isomerism, think molecular formula and number of each atom.
Recall what is different for structural isomers compared with stereoisomers, think connectivity versus spatial arrangement.
Consider one type where the carbon skeleton branches differently, for example butane versus methylpropane.
Consider the other two types, one where the same functional group moves position and one where the functional group itself changes.
walkthrough:
Fix what is identical**
Imagine counting atoms. Both 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane are $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$. Structural isomers always share the same molecular formula, the same numbers of each type of atom.

Fix what is different**
Now imagine joining those atoms up. In structural isomers the order of bonding is different, so the structural or displayed formula is different. This is different from stereoisomers where connectivity is the same but arrangement in space differs.

Name the three families**
Think of three ways to rearrange: change the carbon skeleton, straight chain versus branched, that is chain isomerism. Keep the skeleton and functional group but move it, for example 1-bromobutane versus 2-bromobutane, that is positional isomerism. Keep the atoms but make a different functional group, for example an alcohol versus an ether, that is functional group isomerism.

Final answer: Structural isomers: different molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural / displayed formulae (different connectivity).
Three types: chain / skeletal isomerism; positional / position isomerism; functional group isomerism.

hints: Recall which mechanism primary halogenoalkanes favour versus tertiary halogenoalkanes, think one step versus two steps via a cation.
Compare the intermediate that would form from $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$ with that from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
Link stability to the number of alkyl groups donating electrons by the positive inductive effect.
walkthrough:
Assign the mechanisms**
Reaction 1 with 1-bromobutane, a primary halogenoalkane, goes by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ in one concerted step. The tertiary isomer, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$, goes by $\text{S}_\text{N}1$. That means Br leaves first to give a carbocation, then $\text{OH}^-$ attacks.

Explain why the tertiary path can afford a cation**
Picture $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$. The positive carbon is joined to three methyl groups. Each alkyl group pushes electron density toward the cation by the +I inductive effect, spreading and reducing the charge density. That stabilises the intermediate so the two step route is viable.

Explain why the primary path cannot**
Now picture $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$. There is only one alkyl group to donate electrons, so the +I effect is very limited and the primary cation is too unstable to form easily. So 1-bromobutane avoids the cation and reacts in one $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ step instead.

Final answer: Mechanism: $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ / nucleophilic substitution unimolecular.
$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$ forms a stable tertiary carbocation intermediate, whereas 1-bromobutane (primary) would form an unstable primary cation so goes $\text{S}_\text{N}2$.
Stability due to three alkyl / methyl groups with +I inductive electron donation (versus only one alkyl group in primary, with much less donation).

hints: Recall what stereoisomers share that is more specific than just molecular formula, think about connectivity.
Recall what makes them isomers at all if connectivity is identical, think about arrangement in space.
walkthrough:
Keep connectivity the same**
Do not confuse this with structural isomers. Here the order of bonding is identical. If you draw the structural formula, both stereoisomers look the same.

Change only the 3D arrangement**
The difference is purely spatial. Atoms are arranged differently in space, for example cis versus trans around $\text{C=C}$, or left handed versus right handed around a chiral centre. That spatial difference gives different properties.
Final answer: Stereoisomers have the same molecular and structural formula (same connectivity) but different arrangements of atoms in space.

hints: Recall the two requirements for cis-trans isomerism around a $\text{C=C}$ bond, think restricted rotation plus different groups.
Look closely at each carbon of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$, check whether both carbons carry two different groups.
walkthrough:
Test for cis-trans isomerism**
For cis-trans you need restricted rotation from the $\text{C=C}$ plus two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. Draw $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. The right hand carbon, $\text{=CH}_2$, has two H atoms. Because one end has identical groups, swapping them gives the same structure, so no cis-trans isomers exist.

Test for optical isomerism**
For optical you need a chiral carbon with four different groups. But-1-ene has no such carbon, it is achiral. Its mirror image can be superimposed on itself, so no optical isomers either. With neither type possible, but-1-ene shows no stereoisomerism.

Final answer: But-1-ene does not show stereoisomerism because one carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ has two identical H atoms attached / identical groups on one end, so mirror images are superimposable / molecule is achiral with no chiral centre.

hints: Draw but-1-ene $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$ and consider the two ways H and Cl can add across the double bond.
Recall which carbocation intermediate is more stable, secondary versus primary, to decide which product forms in higher yield.
walkthrough:
Map the two addition routes**
Add $\text{HCl}$ across $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. If H adds to C1 and Cl to C2 you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCH}_3$, which is 2-chlorobutane. If H adds to C2 and Cl to C1 you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, which is 1-chlorobutane. These are positional isomers.

Pick the major product**
Think about carbocations. Adding $\text{H}^+$ to C1 gives a secondary cation on C2, which is more stable than the primary cation formed by adding $\text{H}^+$ to C2. The more stable route dominates, so 2-chlorobutane is X, formed in higher yield, and 1-chlorobutane is Y.

Final answer: X = 2-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCH}_3$ (major product).
Y = 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (minor product).

hints: Look at C2 in 2-chlorobutane and count how many different groups are attached to decide between cis-trans and optical.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCH}_3$. Carbon 2 is bonded to H, Cl, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, four different groups. That is a chiral centre, so X exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images. That is optical isomerism.
Final answer: Optical isomerism.

hints: Draw C2 of 2-chlorobutane with its four groups using solid wedge for coming out and hashed wedge for going back.
To get the second stereoisomer, reflect the first in a mirror or swap any two groups on the chiral centre while keeping the rest the same.
walkthrough:
Draw one enantiomer clearly**
Put the chiral C2 in the centre. Show $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ as straight bonds, Cl as a solid wedge (coming out) and H as a hashed wedge (going back), or any consistent conventional 3D pattern. Label the groups so all four are visible.

Draw its mirror image**
Now draw the exact mirror reflection, for example keep everything the same but swap the wedge and dash, so Cl goes back and H comes out. The two drawings must have the same connectivity but be non-superimposable, that is the pair of optical isomers of 2-chlorobutane.
Final answer: Two 3D structures of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCH}_3$ drawn with wedge / dash at C2, one being the non-superimposable mirror image of the other (enantiomers).
